- PGPPublicKey.join, and with it PGPPublicKeyRing.join and OpenPGPCertificate.join, took two signatures for copies of one another when their signature values matched, and kept the one it already held. A copy of a genuine revocation with its signature type or hashed subpackets rewritten and the signature value left as it was no longer verifies but still matched, so once it had been merged, or when it came first in the same update, the genuine revocation was discarded as its duplicate and the key, subkey or user ID stayed usable. Two signatures are now merged only when they differ in no more than their unhashed subpackets, and PGPSignature.join refuses any other pair. The merge also added to the user ID signature lists of the key it was given, changing the first ring passed to PGPPublicKeyRing.join (github #2508), and lost the value of a version 4 signature carried as a native encoding rather than as MPIs (Ed25519), so that merging a version 4 Ed25519 certificate with a copy of itself gave a ring that could not be encoded; both are corrected.

- PGPPublicKeyRing.join and PGPPublicKey.join, which merge a certificate with another copy of it (OpenPGPCertificate.join merges through them), matched each signature of the copy by scanning the signatures already held, every comparison re-encoding the hashed subpackets and signature value of both, so a merge was quadratic in the number of signatures: two copies of one user ID carrying 20,000 distinct third-party certifications each took over a minute to merge, and anyone can attach certifications to a certificate on a keyserver, as the 2019 flooding of SKS certificates did by the tens of thousands. PGPSignature.join, which a merge applies to every signature both copies carry, likewise scanned the first signature's unhashed subpackets - an area the signature does not cover, so one anyone can fill - for each of the second's, about half a second per shared signature for two full areas, and PGPPublicKeyRing.join looked each key of the first certificate up in the second by a scan. The signatures already held are now indexed once by what two copies of a signature share, the user IDs by value, the second certificate's keys by key ID and the unhashed subpackets through a set. The indexes are ordered trees rather than hash tables: a merge never verifies a signature, so a flooded copy can give every certification one signature value, a user attribute of two identical subpackets hashes to zero, and the hash of a user ID or subpacket's bytes admits multicollisions, any of which drives a hash table's lookups into its collision fallback and the merge back to quadratic. A merge is now O(n log n) in the signatures, user IDs and subpackets of the two copies on every JRE. The merged certificate carries the same content in the same order as before, except that the keys only the second certificate carries now follow in the order it carries them rather than in hash order; the jdk1.3 distribution's PGPPublicKeyRing.join does the same.

- org.bouncycastle.mime.Headers joined folded header lines by String concatenation, copying the whole header accumulated so far for every continuation line, so parsing a long folded header was quadratic in its length: a 1 MB header block of short continuation lines in a message given to BasicMimeParser or the S/MIME parsers took about 17 seconds of CPU, and the block is unbounded. The lines are now appended to a StringBuilder, with the same resulting header values.

-- The ASN.1 parsers for the SEQUENCE types in the X.509, PKCS, OCSP, CMS, CRMF, CMP, ESF, TSP, EAC, DVCS, CMC and ESS packages, and some in the BC, X9 and UA packages, accepted optional fields more than once or out of definition order, and many did not check a tagged field's tag number or ignored elements after the last field. Where a field was repeated, one copy silently replaced the other: a TBSCertificate with two extensions blocks parsed using the first, which also got round the duplicate-extension check, and a second signerInfos SET in a CMS or PKCS#7 SignedData, a repeated PKIMessage protection, and a repeated TSTInfo nonce or accuracy each replaced the first; an OCSPRequest, OCSPResponse or Request with an extra element silently dropped its optionalSignature, responseBytes or singleRequestExtensions, and a TBSRequest its requestExtensions; and an EAC CV certificate accepted its body and signature in either order and more than once, the last copy being used, and its body's data objects in any order; and DVCSCertInfo silently ignored a trailing element that did not parse as Extensions. Each optional field is now accepted at most once, in definition order and with its tag checked, and anything left over is rejected; TBSCertificate.reviewStructure() reports the same problems. RecipientKeyIdentifier also read an OtherKeyAttribute given without a date from the wrong position, and SigPolicyQualifierInfo failed with an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when its qualifier was missing. The GOST 28147/R 34.10 transport types, ECC-CMS-SharedInfo, MQVuserKeyingMaterial, IetfAttrSyntax, the SigI PersonalData, the ISIS-MTT NamingAuthority, ProfessionInfo and ProcurationSyntax, and the deprecated X509Extensions now follow the same rules, ProcurationSyntax requiring its signingFor field, and the streaming SignedData, EnvelopedData, AuthEnvelopedData and AuthenticatedData parsers reject an element after their last field once it has been read, with AuthenticatedDataParser now checking the digestAlgorithm tag; the IetfAttrSyntax acceptance of an untagged policyAuthority, as written by VOMS, is kept. AttributeCertificateInfo takes issuerUniqueID and extensions once each and in that order, so a second extensions block no longer replaces the first, ECPrivateKey and ECPrivateKeyStructure take parameters [0] and publicKey [1] once each and in order, OtherName requires its value to carry context tag [0], CertificationRequestInfo checks the attributes tag while still accepting a request that omits the field, and BasicConstraints rejects trailing elements. PEMParser, which had been handing an EC PRIVATE KEY block holding a PKCS#8 PrivateKeyInfo on as an ECPrivateKey wrapping the whole structure, now reads such a block as the PrivateKeyInfo it is and recovers the public key it carries. The PKCS#12 and PKCS#7 types in org.bouncycastle.asn1.pkcs (ContentInfo, SafeBag, CertBag, CRLBag, SecretBag, EncryptedData, Pfx, MacData and the PBE, PBKDF2, PBES2, PBMAC1, RC2, DH, RSA private key, EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo, IssuerAndSerialNumber, Attribute and CertificationRequest types) now check the [0] tag where they have one and bound the element count, so trailing elements are rejected. Relates to github #2516.
